fa24_mt2_MT2.1.title: MT2.1 - Rotation! Rotation! Rotation!
fa24_mt2_MT2.1.description: Studies rotation matrices, their powers, and dynamic systems with rotation and exponential decay. Combines eigenvalue analysis with geometric transformations.
concepts: Rotation matrix: R(θ) = [[cos θ, -sin θ],[sin θ, cos θ]]

problem_statement.matrix: R = [[cos θ, -sin θ],[sin θ, cos θ]]
problem_statement.part_b: Compute Gramian G_R = R^T R, interpret for columns and rows
problem_statement.part_d: Analyze z(n) = (1/2)^n [[cos(nπ/2), -sin(nπ/2)],[sin(nπ/2), cos(nπ/2)]] z(0), find limit

part_a.answer: R^(-1) = [[cos θ, sin θ],[-sin θ, cos θ]] = R^T = R(-θ)
part_a.geometric_explanation: Inverse of rotation by θ is rotation by -θ. For orthogonal matrices, inverse equals transpose.

part_b.calculation: G_R = R^T R = [[cos²θ + sin²θ, -cos θ sin θ + sin θ cos θ],[-cos θ sin θ + sin θ cos θ, sin²θ + cos²θ]] = I
part_b.column_interpretation: Columns of R are orthonormal: ⟨r₁,r₁⟩ = ⟨r₂,r₂⟩ = 1 and ⟨r₁,r₂⟩ = 0
part_b.row_interpretation: Since G_R = I also means RR^T = I, rows are also orthonormal

part_c.approach: Use eigenvalue decomposition or direct multiplication pattern
pattern_observation: General pattern: R^n rotates by nθ
part_c.proof: By induction or eigenvalue analysis: eigenvalues are e^(±iθ) with |λ| = 1

part_d.pattern: Spiraling inward, rotating 90° each step while decaying by factor 1/2
part_d.geometric_description: Exponential decay with rotation creates inward spiral to origin

formulas: Rotation matrix: R(θ) = [[cos θ, -sin θ],[sin θ, cos θ]]
Orthogonality: R^T R = RR^T = I
Matrix power: R(θ)^n = R(nθ)
Eigenvalues of rotation: λ = e^(±iθ) = cos θ ± i sin θ
Spiral dynamics: r(n) = ρ^n e^(inθ) where ρ < 1 gives inward spiral

fa24_mt2_MT2.2.title: MT2.2 - Triangular Matrices
fa24_mt2_MT2.2.description: Explores properties of triangular matrices including invertibility conditions and the four fundamental subspaces.
concepts: Four fundamental subspaces: N(A), C(A), N(A^T), C(A^T)

problem_statement.part_a: Prove upper-triangular U is invertible iff diagonal entries are nonzero
problem_statement.part_b: For A = [[1,0,0],[2,0,0],[3,2,1]], find bases for all 4 fundamental subspaces
problem_statement.part_c: For A = [[1,0,0],[2,3,0],[4,5,6]], find inverse matrix B

part_a.given: Lower-triangular L invertible ⟺ all diagonal entries nonzero
proof: Key insight: If L is lower-triangular, then L^T is upper-triangular
Given: L invertible ⟺ ℓᵢᵢ ≠ 0 for all i
For upper-triangular U, consider L = U^T (lower-triangular)
By given result: L = U^T invertible ⟺ diagonal(L) all nonzero
So: U^T invertible ⟺ uᵢᵢ ≠ 0 for all i
Therefore: U invertible ⟺ U^T invertible ⟺ uᵢᵢ ≠ 0 for all i ✓

part_b.rank_analysis: rank(A) = 2 (columns 1 and 3 are independent, column 2 is zero)

part_c.verification: Can verify BA = I as well

formulas: Null space: N(A) = {x ∈ ℝⁿ : Ax = 0}
Column space: C(A) = span{columns of A}
Left null space: N(A^T) = {y ∈ ℝᵐ : A^T y = 0}
Row space: C(A^T) = span{rows of A}
Rank-nullity: rank(A) + nullity(A) = n
Orthogonality: C(A) ⊥ N(A^T), C(A^T) ⊥ N(A)
Transpose-inverse: (A^T)^(-1) = (A^(-1))^T

fa24_mt2_MT2.3.title: MT2.3 - Solving Systems with Singular Matrices
fa24_mt2_MT2.3.description: Analyzes systems Ax = b where A is singular (not invertible). Studies conditions for solution existence and uniqueness using fundamental subspaces.

problem_statement.part_a: Explain why A is not invertible
problem_statement.part_b: Solve Ax = b for b = [1, 12]^T. Does unique solution exist?
problem_statement.part_c: Solve Ax = b for b = [2, 6]^T. Does unique solution exist?

part_a.observation: Second column is -2 times the first column: [-2, -6]^T = -2[1, 3]^T
part_a.answer: A is not invertible because its columns are linearly dependent (rank 1), equivalently det(A) = 0
part_a.geometric_interpretation: Columns of A lie on same line through origin, so image is 1-dimensional

consistency_check.calculation: Need b = α[1, 3]^T for some α

part_b.explanation: The vector b = [1, 12]^T is not in the column space of A. For a solution to exist, b must be a linear combination of A's columns.

general_solution.form: x = x_p + x_n where x_n ∈ N(A)

part_c.answer: Solution exists: x = [2+2t, t]^T for any t ∈ ℝ. Two linearly independent solutions: [2, 0]^T and [4, 1]^T

formulas: Invertibility: A invertible ⟺ rank(A) = n ⟺ det(A) ≠ 0
Consistency: Ax = b has solution ⟺ b ∈ C(A)
General solution: x = x_particular + x_nullspace
Solution uniqueness: Unique ⟺ N(A) = {0} ⟺ rank(A) = n
Rank-nullity: rank(A) + dim(N(A)) = n

fa24_mt2_MT2.4.title: MT2.4 - QR Decomposition
fa24_mt2_MT2.4.description: Applies the Gram-Schmidt algorithm to decompose matrix A into orthogonal matrix Q and upper-triangular matrix R.
concepts: Computing R from Q and A

problem_statement.part_b: Determine upper-triangular matrix R such that A = QR

Q_matrix.note: The given Q has columns in different order or signs may differ (both valid)

part_b.formula: Since A = QR, then R = Q^T A
part_b.reason: For orthogonal Q: Q^T Q = I, so Q^T A = Q^T(QR) = R
part_b.verification_upper_triangular: R has zeros below diagonal, confirming upper-triangular structure ✓
part_b.alternative_computation: Can also compute R directly: r_ij = ⟨q_i, a_j⟩ for i ≤ j

formulas: QR decomposition: A = QR where Q^T Q = I and R upper-triangular
Gram-Schmidt: v_k = a_k - Σ_{i=1}^{k-1} ⟨a_k, q_i⟩q_i, then q_k = v_k/‖v_k‖
Computing R: R = Q^T A (when Q is orthogonal)
R entries: r_ij = ⟨q_i, a_j⟩ for i ≤ j
Orthogonality check: ⟨q_i, q_j⟩ = δ_ij (Kronecker delta)

fa24_mt2_MT2.5.title: MT2.5 - Discrete-Time Fourier Series (DTFS)
fa24_mt2_MT2.5.description: Analyzes properties of DTFS for periodic discrete-time signals, including symmetry properties and applications of Parseval's identity.
concepts: Conjugate symmetry and purely imaginary coefficients
Computing DTFS coefficients from signal samples

problem_statement.part_a_i: For odd real-valued p-periodic signal x, show X_{-k} = -X_k
problem_statement.part_b_ii: Express x(n) = α sin(βn), find α and β

part_a_i.given: x is real-valued, odd (x(-n) = -x(n)), and p-periodic
part_a_i.start_with_analysis: X_k = (1/p) Σ_{n∈ℤ_p} x(n) e^(-ik ω₀ n) where ω₀ = 2π/p

apply_negative_k.formula: X_{-k} = (1/p) Σ_{n∈ℤ_p} x(n) e^(ik ω₀ n)
apply_negative_k.substitution: X_{-k} = (1/p) Σ_{m∈ℤ_p} x(-m) e^(-ik ω₀ m)

part_a_i.conclusion: X_{-k} = -X_k, so DTFS coefficients are odd in k

part_a_ii.goal: Show X_k = iβ for some real β (purely imaginary)
part_a_ii.use_real_signal: Since x is real: X_{-k} = X̄_k (conjugate)
part_a_ii.conclusion: X_k has no real part, so X_k = i·Im(X_k) is purely imaginary

part_b_i.periodicity: X_{k+3} = X_k, so: X₃ = X₀ = 0, X₄ = X₁ = i√3/3, etc.
part_b_i.answer: X₀ = 0, X₁ = i√3/3, X₂ = -i√3/3 (repeating with period 3)

part_b_ii.use_euler: e^(i2πn/3) - e^(i4πn/3) = [cos(2πn/3) + i sin(2πn/3)] - [cos(4πn/3) + i sin(4πn/3)]
part_b_ii.answer: α = 2√3/3, β = 2π/3 (or equivalently α = -2√3/3, β = 2π/3 depending on sign convention)

formulas: DTFS synthesis: x(n) = Σ_k X_k e^(ik ω₀ n) where ω₀ = 2π/p
DTFS analysis: X_k = (1/p) Σ_n x(n) e^(-ik ω₀ n)
Real signal: X_{-k} = X̄_k (conjugate symmetry)
Odd signal: x(-n) = -x(n) ⇒ X_{-k} = -X_k
Parseval: (1/p) Σ_n |x(n)|² = Σ_k |X_k|²
Euler's formula: e^(iθ) = cos(θ) + i sin(θ)
Sine from exponentials: sin(θ) = (e^(iθ) - e^(-iθ))/(2i)
